title: What is known about 1RB1RA_0LC0RE_1LF1LD_1LA0LA_1LC1RB_---1LC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RA_0LC0RE_1LF1LD_1LA0LA_1LC1RB_---1LC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape. Its run is an odometer with three wheels; it can only halt at the moment the slowest wheel turns over, and only if the fastest one is at one exact position then.
verdict: The question is open. Every time the head reaches a new cell on the right in state B the tape is S(c, a, b) = (10)^c 1^a 0 (10)^b 1 B>0, and a three-line rule (checked against direct simulation) gives the next one: the right block doubles while the pool can pay, a carry turns a pair of the left block into pool, and when the left block is empty the pool becomes the new left block (a reset). With u = b + 1 and m = a/2 + b + 2 this is exactly a doubling map, u ↦ 2u modulo m, whose modulus grows by one at every operation; c counts the wrap-arounds left before the next reset. The machine halts iff a reset happens with 2u = m exactly.

Why a halt is unlikely. The exact map run for 1011 operations (5·1010 visits, far beyond 1030 machine steps) makes 54 resets, none halting; the left block now has tens of billions of pairs. At a reset 2u − m is spread over about m/2 values and one of them halts; the moduli grow geometrically from reset to reset, so the chance of any later halt is about 10−10. That same growth makes resets logarithmically rare (reset k needs about 1.47k operations), and the doubling map has no known shortcut or invariant, so neither a much longer run nor a proof is in sight.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 4,166 cells have been visited and 3,725 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The odometer rule
claims.text: For S(c, a, b) = 0^∞ (10)^c 1^a 0 (10)^b 1 B>0 0^∞ with a even and a ≥ 2, the next right-end visit in state B is: if 2b < a, S(c, a − 2b, 2b + 1) (the right block doubles, eating 1s); if 2b ≥ a and c ≥ 1, apply the rule to (c − 1, 2a + 4, max(b − a/2 − 1, 0)) (a carry: one 10 of the left block becomes 1s); if 2b ≥ a and c = 0, halt when b = a/2 and otherwise apply the rule to (a, 4, b − a/2 − 1) (a reset: the 1s become the new left block). Checked against direct simulation for all c < 6, even 2 ≤ a < 30, b < 34 (2,856 configurations), and on every such visit in the first 3·10<sup>6</sup> steps of the run, which first reaches S(0, 4, 1) at step 43.

claims.title: The building blocks of the odometer, for all parameters
claims.text: Each main move between two visits is a Lean theorem about every value of its counts and every tape in its context: the start of a sweep, a round (two 1s of the pool and one pair of the right block become four 1s of the middle block), the end of a sweep (the doubled block), the carry (a pair of the left block and the middle block become the new pool) and the reset (the middle block becomes the new left block). They are not yet assembled into one statement of the rule.

claims.title: The exact-hit reset halts
claims.text: With pool, left block and right block all empty (0^∞ A> 1 0 1^(4n+1) 0 1^4 0^∞) the machine fills the tape with 1s and stops on the undefined transition (F reading 0), for every n.

claims.title: The odometer is a doubling map
claims.text: With u = b + 1 and m = a/2 + b + 2: 2u < m is a visit with (2u, m + 1); 2u > m is a carry to (2u − m, m + 1) that uses one unit of c, or with c = 0 a reset to c = 2(m − u − 1), u = 2u − m, m = u + 3; 2u = m is a carry to (1, m + 2), or with c = 0 the halt. It agrees with the odometer rule on the first 200,000 visits of the run. m + c = 5 + visits + resets + emptying carries.

claims.title: 54 resets, no halt
claims.text: The doubling map in C (the same first 50,000 visits and the same resets as the Python model) runs 10<sup>11</sup> operations, 50,000,165,924 visits, 54 resets, without a halt. Reset 54 happens at m = 35,143,437,691 with 2u − m = 1,095,845,857 and makes a left block of 34,047,591,832. The smallest (2u − m)/m at a reset is 0.028 (reset 11).

claims.title: A later halt has probability about 10<sup>−10</sup>
claims.text: At a reset 2u − m is one of about m/2 values, one of which halts. The moduli at resets grow by a factor between 1 and 2 (about 1.47 on average), so the chances form a geometric series: about 6/m after a reset at m, 10<sup>−10</sup> after reset 54. The same growth is why resets are logarithmically rare: reset k needs about 1.47<sup>k</sup> operations.

claims.title: Does a reset ever land on 2u = m (b = a/2)?
claims.text: No congruence excludes it: the halting state has predecessors under the map for every even m. Deciding the machine means deciding a chaotic doubling map with a moving modulus.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows whether it halts. The tape is an odometer with three wheels: a fast one that doubles, a middle one that ticks down, and a slow one that resets. In numbers it doubles a counter u modulo a modulus m that grows by one each time. The machine can only halt at a reset, and only if the doubling lands exactly on m at that moment. In 54 resets that has never happened, and the target keeps getting smaller.

facts.text: The odometer as a doubling map; m grows by one each operation.
No halt in 10<sup>11</sup> operations of the exact map.

sections.heading: Three wheels
html: Each time the head pushes the tape one cell further right in state B, the tape reads (10)^c 1^a 0 (10)^b 1: a left block of c pairs, a pool of a ones, and a right block of b pairs.
• Fast wheel. If the pool is big enough (2b < a), one sweep doubles the right block, b ↦ 2b + 1, paying 2b ones from the pool.
• Middle wheel. If the pool is too small and c ≥ 1, one 10 of the left block is turned into ones: the pool becomes 2a + 4 and b drops by a/2 + 1; then the fast wheel tries again.

• Slow wheel. If the pool is too small and the left block is empty, the whole pool becomes the new left block (c = a), a new pool of 4 starts, and b drops by a/2 + 1 — unless b is exactly a/2, and then the machine halts.

So the run is a sequence of resets, each one creating a left block as long as the pool was. From blank tape the first left blocks are 2, 8, 4, 24, 52, 44, 120, …; after 1011 operations there have been 54 resets and the latest left block is 34,047,591,832 pairs long.

At a reset the fast wheel can be on any of roughly a/3 positions, and only one halts. The chances shrink as the blocks grow, so the total chance that the machine ever halts is tiny (around one in ten billion from here on), but nobody can rule it out.

sections.heading: Doubling modulo a growing number
html: Write u = b + 1 and m = a/2 + b + 2. Then all three wheels become one line: double u, and if it reaches m, subtract m; then add one to m. A doubling that stays below m is a turn of the fast wheel; one that wraps around is a carry, and uses up one pair of the left block. When the left block is empty the next wrap-around is a reset: the left block is refilled with c = 2(m − u − 1) and the modulus drops to (2u − m) + 3.

The machine halts exactly when a reset finds 2u = m: pool, left block and right block all run out in the same sweep (Lean: halt_R). Any other remainder 2u − m, from 1 up to m, just starts the next lap.

Doubling modulo a number that keeps moving scrambles u thoroughly; nobody knows a formula for where it will be after many operations. The exact map has been run for 1011 operations: 54 resets, with 2u − m never smaller than 2.8% of m at a reset. The moduli at resets grow about 1.47-fold each time (reset 54 is at m = 35,143,437,691), so each further reset costs half as much again as everything before it, and the chance of an exact hit, about 2 in m, shrinks just as fast: about 10−10 for all later resets together. Most likely the machine never halts; that is an estimate, not a proof.

explainer.title: An odometer that might stop on one exact number

family: three-wheel odometer = doubling map with a growing modulus
summary: An odometer that is exactly a doubling map: u ↦ 2u modulo m, m growing by one each operation, the left block counting the wrap-arounds allowed before a reset; it halts iff a reset happens with 2u = m. No halt in 10^11 operations (54 resets); heuristically about 10^-10 for a later halt; open.
